title: Let the model choose its augmentations
question: Why keep sampling augmentations blindly when the model can tell us which ones it currently finds difficult?
mechanism: EvolutionAugment samples candidate augmentation policies, evaluates them against the current classifier, and selects difficult examples for the training update. The selection changes as the model learns. We explored selection for individual examples as well as whole batches.
contribution: I mentored the project through regular meetings and technical guidance. The work developed from one of the MSc directions I was supervising; the student built and evaluated the method.
outcome: An implemented method, classification experiments and an MSc dissertation. Evaluating more candidates adds forward-pass cost, so augmentation quality has to be considered alongside training throughput.
discuss: The difference between an example being difficult and being useful to learn from.
When per-example policy selection earns its additional computation.

title: Image translation without starting from scratch
question: Can we reuse what large pretrained models already know to learn a new visual translation from much less data?
mechanism: The project combined CLIP representations, a pretrained StyleGAN2 generator and a learned translation module. A CycleGAN-style objective encouraged consistency in CLIP feature space. Earlier experiments with DALL-E components helped narrow the architecture to Style-CycleGAN.
contribution: I provided weekly supervision and technical suggestions as the architecture and experiments developed. The student implemented and evaluated the translation systems; we were reusing pretrained components, not training those foundation models from scratch.
outcome: Implemented architectures and an MSc dissertation. Some routes did not work, and numerical image-quality measures did not settle every question about whether the translated image preserved the right content.
discuss: What a feature-space cycle loss preserves, and what it can let disappear.
Why freezing weights does not necessarily remove the cost of backpropagating through a model.

title: Adversarially choosing the training view
question: Instead of attacking individual pixels, what if the adversary searched over meaningful transformations of an image?
mechanism: The project made augmentations such as rotation, masked noise and cutout differentiable, then optimised their parameters to challenge the classifier. Constraints on those transformations mattered: an image that no longer contains the class is a rather different training problem.
contribution: I proposed the direction and provided the main day-to-day supervision. I also supplied an existing augmentation-code resource and helped the student reason about the implementation and experiments.
outcome: Implemented methods and image-classification experiments documented in a dissertation. The inner optimisation made training cost an important part of the comparison.
discuss: How to make an augmentation difficult without destroying the information needed to label it.
Comparing robustness at equal wall-clock cost, not just equal numbers of epochs.

title: Which examples should an imbalanced classifier see?
question: Can the model's current mistakes guide a curriculum towards classes it is neglecting?
mechanism: We investigated loss-driven curricula for imbalanced image classification. The implemented procedure cached losses, ranked examples and selected a subset for backward passes, with comparisons across convolutional networks and a vision transformer.
contribution: I supervised the dissertation and helped with technical direction and experimental design. That included thinking through baselines, data splits and the difference between selecting difficult examples and balancing classes.
outcome: A completed dissertation with mixed findings. Training loss alone was not a dependable way to repair class imbalance; its usefulness depended on the setting.
discuss: High loss can mean a useful learning opportunity, insufficient exposure, or an unhelpful outlier. How do we distinguish them?
Controlling the backward-pass budget when comparing a curriculum with class-balanced sampling.

title: DamageGAN: generate the damage we rarely see
question: Could synthetic satellite images help a classifier recognise underrepresented levels of building damage?
mechanism: A class-conditioned pix2pix model generated building-damage imagery from the xBD dataset. The useful test was whether adding those images helped a downstream damage classifier, rather than whether the samples simply looked convincing.
contribution: I supervised the team and helped shape the evaluation: classifier comparisons, augmentation controls, repeated measurements and separating transfer-learning effects from the contribution of generated data.
outcome: An implemented project and manuscript. The study did not establish a clear overall classification improvement. That left an important question: was missing data really the bottleneck, or was the classifier failing to use the surrounding scene?
discuss: Why visually realistic samples can still be poor training data.
The circular difficulty of learning to generate a class for which we have very few real examples.

title: Generating plausible electricity demand
question: A generated demand curve can look reasonable. Does it also preserve the variation and temporal structure we need?
mechanism: The team used a conditional convolutional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty to generate electricity-consumption time series. Evaluation looked at conditional consistency, distributions and autocorrelation rather than relying on a single score.
contribution: I helped refine the research questions and evaluation, then continued supervising development beyond the coursework. Follow-up discussions explored how to condition generation on individual customers.
outcome: A completed coursework study, followed by proposals to test diversity and generalisation to unseen customers.
discuss: A classifier recognising the intended category does not tell us whether the generator covers the distribution.
How to hold out customers, rather than adjacent time windows, when testing generalisation.

title: Give image translation a sense of relationships
question: Can relational processing help a translation model preserve how the parts of an image fit together?
mechanism: We explored relational modules inside image-to-image translation systems, including where to put them in CycleGAN generators and discriminators. Cat-to-dog translation gave us a concrete setting in which texture and semantic structure can pull in different directions.
contribution: I implemented and supplied relational components for both the discriminator and generator, and helped the team integrate them and reason about tensor dimensions. The students integrated the components and ran the broader experiments.
outcome: The relational components were integrated into the translation models and explored in experiments. Component-wise ablations remained a proposed next step.
discuss: Whether relational structure is more useful in the generator, the discriminator, or both.
How to separate changes in visual quality from changes in semantic consistency.

title: Capsules, routing and the shape of a network
question: What does capsule routing buy us once we also give the competing networks sensible depth and connectivity?
mechanism: The project compared capsule networks with conventional convolutional models and explored deeper capsules, routing iterations and skip connections. Pose-related tasks added another complication: a symmetric object may admit more than one sensible orientation.
contribution: I reviewed code, advised on skip connections and supplied my TensorFlow multi-GPU training scaffold. The students developed the models and experiments.
outcome: Implemented models and experiments comparing routing, depth and connectivity. The project explored architectural trade-offs rather than establishing a universal winner.
discuss: Separating the effect of routing from depth, connectivity and training choices.
Choosing a loss for angles when orientation wraps around and objects can be symmetric.

title: Teach the classifier where to look
question: Does learning to localise a finding help a chest-X-ray model generalise when classifying it?
mechanism: A shared DenseNet encoder fed classification and localisation branches. The project compared architectural and loss choices to investigate whether the auxiliary spatial supervision helped pneumonia classification.
contribution: I tutored the original group, continued supervising the research and contributed to the manuscript, architecture discussions and evaluation design.
outcome: Completed comparisons and a co-authored manuscript draft. This was a research study, not a clinically deployed diagnostic system.
discuss: When an auxiliary task helps a shared representation and when it causes negative transfer.
Whether the information gained from localisation justifies the additional annotation effort.

title: Evolving both the policy and how we search
question: Can an evolutionary search adapt its own search behaviour while learning a neural control policy?
mechanism: The team investigated neuroevolution on Atari and MuJoCo tasks, comparing population sizes, crossover and a hierarchical genetic approach to adapting search parameters.
contribution: I provided tutoring and research guidance through the semester, reviewed the report and invited the team to continue developing the work afterwards.
outcome: A completed coursework report with mixed findings. The hierarchical approach left useful avenues to explore, but was not sufficiently tuned to support a general performance claim.
discuss: What should evolve: the policy weights, mutation scales, or the search procedure itself?
Making an evolutionary search and a policy-gradient method comparable under a fixed compute budget.

title: Different words, the same meaning?
question: How do we generate genuinely different paraphrases without quietly changing what the sentence says?
mechanism: The project used pretrained GPT-2 and RoBERTa components within a conditional variational autoencoder, comparing them with an LSTM paraphrasing baseline. Diversity, grammar and semantic control were separate concerns.
contribution: I guided the group and subsequently invited them to develop the project towards a paper. Our follow-up discussions considered other pretrained-model routes without treating those proposed extensions as completed work.
outcome: A completed report described improvements over its baseline alongside grammatical errors and weaknesses in preserving meaning.
discuss: Why lexical diversity can reward a paraphrase for becoming less faithful.
Which limitations come from the representation, the latent objective and the decoder.

title: Transliterate the sound, not the meaning
question: For English-to-Chinese transliteration, which representations preserve the information the task actually needs?
mechanism: The project explored attention-based sequence models, phonetic auxiliary information and CharacterBERT-derived embeddings. The task asks for a sound-preserving rendering rather than an ordinary semantic translation.
contribution: I tutored the project and helped with framing and review as part of the MLP research-development work.
outcome: An implemented coursework project. Working notes identified a training-schedule confound in an apparent embedding advantage, making matched training conditions important to the interpretation.
discuss: When a representation rich in semantics is missing the information a phonetic task needs.
Matching training schedules and tuning budgets before attributing a gain to pretraining.

title: Use CLIP to make faces follow descriptions
question: Can pretrained image–text representations give a small text-to-face dataset a better starting point?
mechanism: The team modified AttnGAN with CLIP sentence representations and similarity losses, while retaining word-level components. Changing the conditioning and changing the objective were different experiments, not one interchangeable use of CLIP.
contribution: I advised on using CLIP text embeddings in the generator and image embeddings in the discriminator, tutored the group and later invited them to develop the work into a paper.
outcome: Completed comparisons included unsuccessful variants, making the choice of where and how to use CLIP central to the interpretation. We discussed developing the work into a paper.
discuss: Whether an improvement comes from better conditioning or a better learning signal.
A plausible face is not necessarily a face that matches the description.

title: Does the model understand the image and text together?
question: A meme can mean something that neither the picture nor its caption means alone. Does the classifier notice?
mechanism: The project investigated CLIP representations for hateful-meme detection, comparing image-only, text-only and joint encoder choices. Those comparisons help expose whether a model benefits from the interaction or mostly exploits one modality.
contribution: I tutored the group and helped guide the project scope and the comparisons between image, text and joint encoders.
outcome: Classifier training and a coursework report, with cross-dataset transfer left for follow-up.
discuss: How to detect a unimodal shortcut in an apparently multimodal system.
What a within-dataset score leaves unresolved about transfer to a different collection of memes.
